analysis.one_liner: Requires disclosure of dark money, restricts foreign and super PAC spending, and adds public financing for Senate campaigns.
analysis.headline: The democracy reform bill, backed by 16 senators, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This was an omnibus democracy bill. It would have required groups spending money on campaign ads to name their donors, extended the ban on foreign election money to foreign-influenced U.S. corporations, cracked down on super PAC coordination with candidates, replaced the gridlocked Federal Election Commission with a new enforcement agency, restricted the revolving door between financial regulators and the industry they police, and required the President and Vice President to disclose their tax returns and divest conflicting financial interests. It also would have created generous public matching funds for small campaign donations, required every state to draw congressional maps through an independent commission, and made it easier to register and vote through automatic and same-day registration and vote by mail.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters and small donors gain the most. Disclosure rules would let citizens see who is bankrolling the political ads they watch; small-dollar matching funds and a refundable tax credit would let candidates win on small contributions instead of courting big check-writers; independent redistricting would end the practice of legislators drawing their own safe districts; and automatic, same-day registration and vote-by-mail provisions would make voting easier for working people whose schedules make it hard to get to the polls. Candidates who rely on grassroots support, rather than access to wealthy bundlers, would also gain.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters, small donors, and grassroots candidates

how_it_helps.text: Any corporation, nonprofit, or other group spending more than $10,000 on campaign communications would have to file a statement, within 24 hours of crossing disclosure thresholds, listing each donor who gave $10,000 or more, including beneficial owners behind shell entities.

The existing ban on foreign nationals contributing to elections would be extended to U.S. corporations that are foreign-controlled or foreign-influenced, with CEOs required to certify compliance under penalty of perjury.

Spending coordinated between candidates and super PACs would be treated as an illegal campaign contribution, with penalties of up to 300% of the excess, and federal candidates and officeholders would be barred from fundraising for super PACs.
The Federal Election Commission would be replaced with a Federal Election Administration charged with actually enforcing election laws.

Financial-services regulators would be barred from using their position to benefit former employers or clients, and other revolving-door rules would slow the movement of officials into the industry they supervised.

The President and Vice President would be required to disclose their financial interests, including tax returns, to Congress and the Office of Government Ethics, and to divest interests posing potential conflicts.

Presidential campaigns accepting public financing would get 600% matching funds for small contributions, and Senate candidates could opt into a 'Fair Elections' public financing program, backed by a refundable tax credit for small Senate campaign contributions.
Every state would be required to draw congressional districts through an independent commission, and if no commission plan is enacted, a plan developed by a three-judge federal court.
States would have to allow automatic voter registration, same-day registration, and vote by mail in federal elections.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would have fallen mainly on concentrated interests: super PACs, dark-money nonprofits, trade associations, and foreign-influenced corporations would lose the ability to spend without naming their funders; wealthy donors and lobbyist bundlers would matter less when small donations are multiplied six-fold with public matching funds; financial firms would face restrictions on hiring former regulators; and lobbyists would face tighter registration and bundling disclosure. Taxpayers would also fund the public financing programs through a dedicated revenue provision in the bill.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big donors, dark-money groups, financial firms, lobbyists

drawbacks.text: Public financing costs public money: the bill provides 600% matching funds for presidential campaigns, a Fair Elections program for Senate races, and a refundable tax credit for Senate campaign contributions, all funded through a dedicated revenue provision.

The redistricting mandate would strip mapdrawing from elected legislatures and, if a commission's plan is not enacted, hand the job to the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, which critics would object to as unelected actors drawing political maps far from the affected states.

Replacing the Federal Election Commission with a new Federal Election Administration would concentrate enforcement power in a single new agency, which defenders of the current structure argue risks one-sided administration of election law.

The donor-disclosure rules would apply to tax-exempt advocacy groups and labor organizations, and groups concerned with donor privacy argue that publishing names of people who fund political speech can chill lawful participation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits to ordinary voters—knowing who pays for political ads, diminishing the power of big checks, easier registration and voting, and conflicted-interest rules at the top of government—are broad and durable. The real costs are money: public financing spends taxpayer dollars on campaigns, and that trade-off is a fair matter of debate. The disclosure provisions are the strongest good-faith flashpoint, since they reach tax-exempt advocacy groups; the bill's generous thresholds (disclosure only for donors giving $10,000 or more) mitigate but do not eliminate the donor-privacy concern. On balance, the design targets secret political spending and structural conflicts of interest rather than ordinary political activity.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and sat there, with no hearing, markup, or floor vote, until the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Udall introduced the We the People Democracy Reform Act of 2017 in the Senate on September 27, 2017, joined by 14 other senators as original cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
Sixteen senators total supported the bill: 15 Democrats and 1 Independent.
No further action—no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote—ever occurred, and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The beneficiaries of the status quo: undisclosed big donors and the super PACs and dark-money groups they fund, foreign-influenced corporations seeking to spend on U.S. elections, financial firms that hire former regulators, lobbyists and bundlers, and officeholders whose districts are drawn by fellow legislators. Nothing changed for anyone, but the people the bill would have constrained were spared the new rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big-money donors and secret political spenders

for.name: Sen. Tom Udall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it, joining it to a package of disclosure, public financing, redistricting, and voting-rights reforms.

for.name: 15 Senate Democrats and 1 Independent cosponsor
for.role: Cosponsors including Sens. Merkley, Durbin, Leahy, Baldwin, Gillibrand, Hirono, King (I), Klobuchar, Markey, Van Hollen, Franken, Wyden, Warren, and Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors at introduction; none had a committee role that could advance the bill.

against.name: Chair, Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee chair with sole control over whether the bill got a hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: After the bill was referred to the Finance Committee, the committee took no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling the Senate floor and agenda
against.what_they_did: Never brought campaign finance and democracy reform legislation to the floor in the 115th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 senators who backed the bill were Democrats plus one Independent who caucuses with them; no Republican cosponsored, and Republicans controlled both the Senate majority and the Finance Committee it was referred to.

industries.industry: Super PACs and dark-money political groups
industries.note: The bill would force these groups to disclose their major donors and would treat spending they coordinate with candidates as illegal contributions. Their interest in remaining unaccountable runs directly against voters' interest in knowing who pays for the ads aimed at them.

industries.industry: Corporations with significant foreign ownership or control
industries.note: They would be banned from spending on U.S. elections, with CEO certifications required. Their interest in keeping that spending channel open runs against the public interest in keeping foreign money out of American elections.

Revolving-door restrictions would bar regulators from working on matters benefiting former employers or clients and slow their movement into private firms. The industry benefits today from the expertise and relationships of former regulators.

Tighter registration rules, expanded disclosure of bundled contributions, and a ban on presidential joint fundraising committees would raise the cost of the access they sell. Their business model depends on influence that these provisions would make visible.

Participating Senate candidates would get reduced broadcast ad rates and standardized ad reporting, cutting into a reliable source of campaign-season revenue, though stations would still carry paid political advertising overall.

Six-times matching funds for small donations and independent redistricting would reduce the leverage of large contributors and of legislators who draw their own districts. This is the bill's central purpose rather than a side effect.
